description: Hi everyone! I'm a 3rd-year Artificial Intelligence and Data Science student interested in AI, data science, web development, and innovative technology.
summary: StillOut There is a free, mobile-friendly web app that introduces students aged 8-14 to the rovers, landers and probes NASA has left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Today these objects reach children as dry spec sheets scattered across NASA databases. Our prototype gives each object a voice: kids explore a Relic Map, tap a pin, and hear the hardware tell its story in first person, adapted to their grade level and available in English, Tamil and Hindi. Every fact is linked to its NASA source, so children learn to check evidence instead of trusting an AI blindly. A Then vs Now slider compares landing-day imagery with orbiter imagery, short science missions (such as why Spirit got stuck) earn badges, and an AR view places a rover on the learner’s desk. A “Write the Last Message” activity turns curiosity into reflection. The project makes space science personal, trustworthy and accessible to regional-language learners.
details:
What it does: StillOut There turns NASA’s left-behind hardware into characters. Learners pick Moon, Mars or deep space on the Relic Map. Each object has a live status tag (Active, Sleeping, Silent, Still travelling). Tapping a pin opens a first-person story at the learner’s grade level (3-5 or 6-8) and language (EN, TA, HI), with a NASA source link on every statement. A Then vs Now slider compares landing-day and orbiter imagery. Science missions test real concepts and award badges. AR lets learners place a 3D model on their desk. Our designed teacher mode adds quizzes, worksheets and NGSS-aligned prompts.

How it works: The prototype uses a curated knowledge base of NASA-verified facts for [5] objects. Stories are written only from those facts, and each sentence keeps its source link. The designed full system uses a Next.js PWA, a FastAPI backend, and retrieval-augmented generation (FAISS or Chroma) so an LLM rewrites only retrieved NASA text. Tools used in the prototype: [React/Vite, Leaflet or Three.js, model-viewer (WebXR AR), Web Speech API, Netlify/Vercel]. Edit this list to match what you actually built.

Impact and benefits: Students get memorable, story-first science. Teachers get ready-made classroom material. Schools with weak internet benefit from the planned offline pack. Tamil and Hindi support reaches regional learners. The project also introduces space heritage and debris ethics.

Creativity: Treating hardware as characters with lifecycle status, “Write the Last Message”, and per-sentence citations set it apart from spec sheets and generic chatbots.

Factors considered: Child safety and trust (verified facts only), accessibility (language, reading level, low bandwidth), and scalability (a new object needs one data entry and one 3D model).

Research basis: RAG (Lewis et al., 2020), hallucination survey (Ji et al., 2023), narrative in science communication (Avraamidou & Osborne, 2009), AR in education (Akçayır & Akçayır, 2017), gamification (Deterding et al., 2011), LROC instrument overview (Robinson et al., 2010).

Future work: Voice narration in Tamil and Hindi, teacher dashboard, offline pack, Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan comparisons, and pilots in 2-3 schools.
